initial_messages.content:
You are an on-call engineer doing a read-only incident investigation.
You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

How to work:
- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

When you have finished, reply without any tool call, using exactly these sections:
## Timeline
## Best-supported cause
## Competing explanation
## Recommended mitigation
## Uncertainty

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not modify production settings or disable payment safety checks.

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.

8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. 15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |

17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18|

20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

input.content:
You are an on-call engineer doing a read-only incident investigation.
You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

When you have finished, reply without any tool call, using exactly these sections:
## Timeline
## Best-supported cause
## Competing explanation
## Recommended mitigation
## Uncertainty

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not modify production settings or disable payment safety checks.

Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |

Task and constraints
Investigate why POST /checkout slowed after the latest release; build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back; do not disable or weaken fraud screening or idempotency checks. All times are UTC. [ticket:L24-L30]

Evidence gathered so far
- Release v2.14.0 rollout began 2026-10-06 14:02:10; migration 0142 was applied at 14:02:55; all instances were healthy and payment client profile v18 loaded at 14:04:00; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09:00. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- Release changes include enabling address validation, increasing cart cache TTL from 30 s to 60 s, and payment profile v18. The payment client changed from request timeout 2000 ms to 8000 ms, max attempts 2 to 4, fixed to exponential backoff, and backoff base 100 ms to 250 ms. Retries cover timeout, HTTP 502, and HTTP 503. Idempotency key reuse remains true. [release-notes:L5-L9] [config-diff:L13-L20] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- On 2026-10-06, orders-db CPU alert fired at 14:15 with value 84% (threshold 75% for 5m); payment-client-error-ratio fired at 14:21 with 4/16 (threshold 10% for 2m); checkout-latency-p95 fired at 14:22 with 17093 ms (threshold 3000 ms for 3m). [alerts-log:L5-L7]
- Orders-db scheduled `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_created_at` ran 14:10-14:41; change log says elevated CPU expected for duration, no table locks, and query latency may rise slightly. [db-change-log:L3-L7]
- Provider reports elevated EU-1 authorization latency beginning approximately 14:18; investigating at 14:23, faulty acquirer connection pool identified at 14:51, affected nodes drained at 15:04, and resolved at 15:09. Provider says impact was approximately 14:18-15:05 and retries with the same idempotency key were not double-charged. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Alerts resolved: orders-db CPU at 14:46 (32%); payment-client-error-ratio at 15:06 (0/12); checkout-latency-p95 at 15:07 (504 ms). [alerts-log:L8-L10] Ticket notes checkout latency was normal again by 15:12 without intervention. [ticket:L17-L20]
- Provider had a separate EU-1 authorization degradation on 2026-10-04, approximately 14:01-14:25. [provider-status:L11-L14] That day, payment-client-error-ratio fired at 14:04 (12/19) and checkout-latency-p95 at 14:11 (4196 ms); both resolved at 14:26. [alerts-log:L1-L4]
- Runbook permits a fully reversible payment-client runtime-profile rollback, applied within ~60 s, with incident commander approval. It requires preserving idempotent retries. Verification is to watch checkout p95 and payment-client error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L10-L22]

Findings so far (provisional)
- Leading hypothesis: provider authorization degradation triggered retries, and v18’s longer timeout and more attempts/backoff prolonged affected checkouts. Timing aligns with provider’s reported 14:18–15:05 impact and the payment/latency alerts; v18 changed precisely those behaviors. This remains unverified against client logs and traces. [config-diff:L30-L47] [provider-status:L5-L9] [alerts-log:L6-L10]
- Main competing explanation: database CPU/reindex contributed to latency. It overlaps the incident, but the change record describes expected elevated CPU and only slight possible query-latency rise; timing alone does not establish it as the primary cause. DB metrics and traces have not been inspected, so it is not ruled out. [db-change-log:L3-L7] [alerts-log:L5-L8]
- Address validation is another release change, but no evidence yet establishes whether it contributed. [release-notes:L5-L7] [config-diff:L16-L20]
- The 2026-10-04 provider degradation and checkout alerts show that gateway-related slowdowns predated v2.14.0; they do not establish the contribution of v18. [provider-status:L11-L14] [alerts-log:L1-L4]

Read per-minute checkout metrics, sampled traces for both dates, payment client logs, and DB metrics to compare latency and request paths, identify retries/timeouts, and assess DB pool/query waits. Check address-service spans if present. Then quantify whether v18 amplified the provider event and whether DB activity explains any independent delay. Task and constraints
Investigate why POST /checkout slowed after the latest release; build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back; do not disable or weaken fraud screening or idempotency checks. All times are UTC. [ticket:L24-L30]

Evidence gathered so far
- Release v2.14.0 rollout began 2026-10-06 14:02:10; migration 0142 was applied at 14:02:55; all instances were healthy and payment client profile v18 loaded at 14:04:00; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09:00. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- Release changes include enabling address validation, increasing cart cache TTL from 30 s to 60 s, and payment profile v18. The payment client changed from request timeout 2000 ms to 8000 ms, max attempts 2 to 4, fixed to exponential backoff, and backoff base 100 ms to 250 ms. Retries cover timeout, HTTP 502, and HTTP 503. Idempotency key reuse remains true. [release-notes:L5-L9] [config-diff:L13-L20] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- On 2026-10-06, orders-db CPU alert fired at 14:15 with value 84% (threshold 75% for 5m); payment-client-error-ratio fired at 14:21 with 4/16 (threshold 10% for 2m); checkout-latency-p95 fired at 14:22 with 17093 ms (threshold 3000 ms for 3m). [alerts-log:L5-L7]
- Orders-db scheduled `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_created_at` ran 14:10-14:41; change log says elevated CPU expected for duration, no table locks, and query latency may rise slightly. [db-change-log:L3-L7]
- Provider reports elevated EU-1 authorization latency beginning approximately 14:18; investigating at 14:23, faulty acquirer connection pool identified at 14:51, affected nodes drained at 15:04, and resolved at 15:09. Provider says impact was approximately 14:18-15:05 and retries with the same idempotency key were not double-charged. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Alerts resolved: orders-db CPU at 14:46 (32%); payment-client-error-ratio at 15:06 (0/12); checkout-latency-p95 at 15:07 (504 ms). [alerts-log:L8-L10] Ticket notes checkout latency was normal again by 15:12 without intervention. [ticket:L17-L20]
- Provider had a separate EU-1 authorization degradation on 2026-10-04, approximately 14:01-14:25. [provider-status:L11-L14] That day, payment-client-error-ratio fired at 14:04 (12/19) and checkout-latency-p95 at 14:11 (4196 ms); both resolved at 14:26. [alerts-log:L1-L4]
- Runbook permits a fully reversible payment-client runtime-profile rollback, applied within ~60 s, with incident commander approval. It requires preserving idempotent retries. Verification is to watch checkout p95 and payment-client error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L10-L22]

Findings so far (provisional)
- Leading hypothesis: provider authorization degradation triggered retries, and v18’s longer timeout and more attempts/backoff prolonged affected checkouts. Timing aligns with provider’s reported 14:18–15:05 impact and the payment/latency alerts; v18 changed precisely those behaviors. This remains unverified against client logs and traces. [config-diff:L30-L47] [provider-status:L5-L9] [alerts-log:L6-L10]
- Main competing explanation: database CPU/reindex contributed to latency. It overlaps the incident, but the change record describes expected elevated CPU and only slight possible query-latency rise; timing alone does not establish it as the primary cause. DB metrics and traces have not been inspected, so it is not ruled out. [db-change-log:L3-L7] [alerts-log:L5-L8]
- Address validation is another release change, but no evidence yet establishes whether it contributed. [release-notes:L5-L7] [config-diff:L16-L20]
- The 2026-10-04 provider degradation and checkout alerts show that gateway-related slowdowns predated v2.14.0; they do not establish the contribution of v18. [provider-status:L11-L14] [alerts-log:L1-L4]

Unresolved questions / next steps
Read per-minute checkout metrics, sampled traces for both dates, payment client logs, and DB metrics to compare latency and request paths, identify retries/timeouts, and assess DB pool/query waits. Check address-service spans if present. Then quantify whether v18 amplified the provider event and whether DB activity explains any independent delay. Consider recommending rollback of only the runtime payment-client profile to v17 as the smallest reversible mitigation, subject to confirming evidence and incident commander approval; do not weaken safety checks. No mitigation has been applied.

Do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back; do not disable or weaken fraud screening or idempotency checks. All times are UTC. [ticket:L24-L30]

The payment client changed from request timeout 2000 ms to 8000 ms, max attempts 2 to 4, fixed to exponential backoff, and backoff base 100 ms to 250 ms. Retries cover timeout, HTTP 502, and HTTP 503. Idempotency key reuse remains true. [release-notes:L5-L9] [config-diff:L13-L20] [config-diff:L30-L47]

Task and constraints
Investigate why POST /checkout slowed after release v2.14.0; build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not change production settings, deploy, roll back, or disable/weaken fraud screening or idempotency. All times are UTC. [ticket:L24-L30]

Evidence gathered
- Release v2.14.0 rollout began 2026-10-06 14:02:10; migration 0142 was applied at 14:02:55; all instances were healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04:00; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09:00. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- v2.14.0 enabled address validation, increased cart cache TTL from 30 s to 60 s, and loaded payment profile v18. Payment settings changed from timeout 2000 ms to 8000 ms, max attempts 2 to 4, fixed to exponential backoff, and backoff base 100 ms to 250 ms. Retries cover timeout, HTTP 502, and HTTP 503; idempotency key reuse remains true. [release-notes:L5-L9] [config-diff:L13-L20] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- Alerts on Oct 6: orders-db CPU fired at 14:15, 84% (threshold 75% for 5m); payment-client error ratio at 14:21, 4/16 (threshold 10% for 2m); checkout p95 at 14:22, 17093 ms (threshold 3000 ms for 3m). They resolved at 14:46 (DB 32%), 15:06 (payment 0/12), and 15:07 (checkout p95 504 ms). [alerts-log:L5-L10]
- Provider reported elevated EU-1 authorization latency beginning approximately 14:18; faulty acquirer pool identified at 14:51, affected nodes drained at 15:04, and provider impact resolved at 15:09 (reported impact approximately 14:18–15:05). [provider-status:L5-L9] Ticket says checkout latency was normal by 15:12 without intervention. [ticket:L17-L20]
- Sampled Oct 6 traces show a normal 14:20 checkout of 451 ms with 336 ms payment authorization and one successful attempt. [traces-2026-10-06:L317-L323] At 14:22, a checkout took 8695 ms: DB cart load 24 ms, address validation 38 ms, fraud screen 34 ms, payment authorization 8562 ms; payment attempt 1 timed out at 8005 ms, attempt 2 succeeded in 306 ms. [traces-2026-10-06:L331-L338] At 14:24, checkout took 8668 ms with payment authorization 8543 ms; attempt 1 timed out at 8005 ms and attempt 2 succeeded in 287 ms. [traces-2026-10-06:L346-L353] Another normal checkout at 14:23 took 412 ms, with payment authorization 288 ms. [traces-2026-10-06:L339-L345]
- Address-validation spans in sampled traces are 22–40 ms, including the 14:22 38 ms span. [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L334] [traces-2026-10-06:L341-L342] [traces-2026-10-06:L348-L349]
- Before release, the payment client reported v17 at 14:00 with 2000 ms timeout, 2 attempts, fixed backoff 100 ms. A sampled v17 request at 14:02:05 timed out at 2004 ms and retried; at 14:02:27 another timed out at 2001 ms then got HTTP 502. [payment-client-log:L2-L7]
- On Oct 4, while release 2.13.3 was running, checkout p95 rose to 4197 ms at 14:02 and remained around 4.2 s in multiple minutes through 14:23; it was 476 ms at 14:24. [checkout-metrics:L32-L58] DB metrics for Oct 4 around that event show query p95 14–18 ms, CPU 26–38%, and pool wait p95 0–1 ms. [db-metrics:L32-L58]
- Orders DB reindex ran Oct 6 from 14:10–14:41; change log expected elevated CPU during the run, no table locks, and only a slight possible query-latency rise. [db-change-log:L3-L7]

Findings so far (some still uncertain)
- Best-supported cause: EU-1 provider authorization degradation triggered payment timeouts; v18’s longer timeout and expanded retries/backoff amplified the wait for affected checkouts. The provider impact overlaps the alerts, and sampled slow traces directly locate most of their duration in payment, including an 8-second timeout followed by a successful retry. [provider-status:L5-L9] [traces-2026-10-06:L331-L338] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- Provider problems predated v2.14.0: on Oct 4, provider degradation coincided with checkout latency and payment-error alerts, when 2.13.3/v17 was in use. This supports provider degradation as an independent trigger, not v18 as the sole cause. [provider-status:L11-L14] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [checkout-metrics:L32-L58] [payment-client-log:L2-L4]
- Main competing explanation, DB CPU/reindex: Oct 6 CPU alert and reindex overlap the incident, so DB contribution is not fully ruled out. However, the Oct 4 DB metrics were normal during a similar gateway-related checkout spike, and sampled Oct 6 slow traces have only 24 ms cart load and 30 ms order persistence versus 8.5 s payment authorization. Oct 6 incident-window DB metrics still need inspection. [alerts-log:L5-L8] [db-metrics:L32-L58] [traces-2026-10-06:L331-L338]
- Address validation is unlikely to explain multi-second sampled delays (22–40 ms spans), but its full contribution has not been evaluated. [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L334] [traces-2026-10-06:L348-L349]

Next steps and mitigation
Read the remainder of checkout and DB metrics (from offset 121), inspect payment-client logs during the Oct 6 impact and more traces from both dates, and compare DB pool/query waits and address-service spans. Quantify how v18 changed retry behavior and assess whether DB activity caused any independent delay.
No mitigation has been applied. Runbook permits a reversible runtime-profile rollback to v17 within about 60 s, with incident commander approval, while preserving idempotent retries. If justified, recommend that as the smallest mitigation; verify checkout p95 and payment error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L10-L22]

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

How to work:
- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

Task and constraints
Investigate why POST /checkout slowed after release v2.14.0; build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not change production settings, deploy, roll back, or disable/weaken fraud screening or idempotency. All times are UTC. [ticket:L24-L30]

Evidence gathered
- Release v2.14.0 rollout began 2026-10-06 14:02:10; migration 0142 was applied at 14:02:55; all instances were healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04:00; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09:00. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- v2.14.0 enabled address validation, increased cart cache TTL from 30 s to 60 s, and loaded payment profile v18. Payment settings changed from timeout 2000 ms to 8000 ms, max attempts 2 to 4, fixed to exponential backoff, and backoff base 100 ms to 250 ms. Retries cover timeout, HTTP 502, and HTTP 503; idempotency key reuse remains true. [release-notes:L5-L9] [config-diff:L13-L20] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- Alerts on Oct 6: orders-db CPU fired at 14:15, 84% (threshold 75% for 5m); payment-client error ratio at 14:21, 4/16 (threshold 10% for 2m); checkout p95 at 14:22, 17093 ms (threshold 3000 ms for 3m). They resolved at 14:46 (DB 32%), 15:06 (payment 0/12), and 15:07 (checkout p95 504 ms). [alerts-log:L5-L10]
- Provider reported elevated EU-1 authorization latency beginning approximately 14:18; faulty acquirer pool identified at 14:51, affected nodes drained at 15:04, and provider impact resolved at 15:09 (reported impact approximately 14:18–15:05). [provider-status:L5-L9] Ticket says checkout latency was normal by 15:12 without intervention. [ticket:L17-L20]
- Sampled Oct 6 traces show a normal 14:20 checkout of 451 ms with 336 ms payment authorization and one successful attempt. [traces-2026-10-06:L317-L323] At 14:22, a checkout took 8695 ms: DB cart load 24 ms, address validation 38 ms, fraud screen 34 ms, payment authorization 8562 ms; payment attempt 1 timed out at 8005 ms, attempt 2 succeeded in 306 ms. [traces-2026-10-06:L331-L338] At 14:24, checkout took 8668 ms with payment authorization 8543 ms; attempt 1 timed out at 8005 ms and attempt 2 succeeded in 287 ms. [traces-2026-10-06:L346-L353] Another normal checkout at 14:23 took 412 ms, with payment authorization 288 ms. [traces-2026-10-06:L339-L345]
- Address-validation spans in sampled traces are 22–40 ms, including the 14:22 38 ms span. [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L334] [traces-2026-10-06:L341-L342] [traces-2026-10-06:L348-L349]
- Before release, the payment client reported v17 at 14:00 with 2000 ms timeout, 2 attempts, fixed backoff 100 ms. A sampled v17 request at 14:02:05 timed out at 2004 ms and retried; at 14:02:27 another timed out at 2001 ms then got HTTP 502. [payment-client-log:L2-L7]
- On Oct 4, while release 2.13.3 was running, checkout p95 rose to 4197 ms at 14:02 and remained around 4.2 s in multiple minutes through 14:23; it was 476 ms at 14:24. [checkout-metrics:L32-L58] DB metrics for Oct 4 around that event show query p95 14–18 ms, CPU 26–38%, and pool wait p95 0–1 ms. [db-metrics:L32-L58]
- Orders DB reindex ran Oct 6 from 14:10–14:41; change log expected elevated CPU during the run, no table locks, and only a slight possible query-latency rise. [db-change-log:L3-L7]

Findings so far (some still uncertain)
- Best-supported cause: EU-1 provider authorization degradation triggered payment timeouts; v18’s longer timeout and expanded retries/backoff amplified the wait for affected checkouts. The provider impact overlaps the alerts, and sampled slow traces directly locate most of their duration in payment, including an 8-second timeout followed by a successful retry. [provider-status:L5-L9] [traces-2026-10-06:L331-L338] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- Provider problems predated v2.14.0: on Oct 4, provider degradation coincided with checkout latency and payment-error alerts, when 2.13.3/v17 was in use. This supports provider degradation as an independent trigger, not v18 as the sole cause. [provider-status:L11-L14] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [checkout-metrics:L32-L58] [payment-client-log:L2-L4]
- Main competing explanation, DB CPU/reindex: Oct 6 CPU alert and reindex overlap the incident, so DB contribution is not fully ruled out. However, the Oct 4 DB metrics were normal during a similar gateway-related checkout spike, and sampled Oct 6 slow traces have only 24 ms cart load and 30 ms order persistence versus 8.5 s payment authorization. Oct 6 incident-window DB metrics still need inspection. [alerts-log:L5-L8] [db-metrics:L32-L58] [traces-2026-10-06:L331-L338]
- Address validation is unlikely to explain multi-second sampled delays (22–40 ms spans), but its full contribution has not been evaluated. [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L334] [traces-2026-10-06:L348-L349]

Next steps and mitigation
Read the remainder of checkout and DB metrics (from offset 121), inspect payment-client logs during the Oct 6 impact and more traces from both dates, and compare DB pool/query waits and address-service spans. Quantify how v18 changed retry behavior and assess whether DB activity caused any independent delay.
No mitigation has been applied. Runbook permits a reversible runtime-profile rollback to v17 within about 60 s, with incident commander approval, while preserving idempotent retries. If justified, recommend that as the smallest mitigation; verify checkout p95 and payment error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L10-L22]

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

The provider impact overlaps the alerts, and sampled slow traces directly locate most of their duration in payment, including an 8-second timeout followed by a successful retry. Oct 6 incident-window DB metrics still need inspection. [alerts-log:L5-L8] [db-metrics:L32-L58] [traces-2026-10-06:L331-L338]

response.content:
## Timeline

- **14:02–14:09:** The v2.14.0 rollout began at 14:02:10, migration 0142 was applied at 14:02:55, and all instances were healthy with payment profile v18 loaded by 14:04. Post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L15-L18]
- **14:10 onward:** The scheduled orders-DB reindex ran until 14:41; its change record anticipated elevated CPU but no table locks and only a possible slight query-latency rise. [db-change-log:L7]
- **Approximately 14:18:** The payment provider’s reported EU-1 impact began. Checkout metrics were near normal at 14:18, then showed elevated latency from 14:19 onward; the checkout p95 alert fired at 14:22. [provider-status:L7-L9] [checkout-metrics:L140-L145] [alerts-log:L7]
- **14:22–14:24:** Sampled traces show the long part of slow checkouts was payment authorization: one took 8,562 ms, including an 8,005 ms timeout followed by a successful retry; another took 8,543 ms with the same timeout-then-success pattern. By comparison, cart load and order persistence took 16–24 ms, address validation 38–39 ms, and fraud screening 34–43 ms. A nearby checkout at 14:23 completed in 412 ms, including 288 ms for payment. [traces-2026-10-06:L331-L353]
- **14:51–15:09:** The provider identified a faulty acquirer connection pool at 14:51, drained affected nodes at 15:04, and reported the impact resolved at 15:09. Checkout metrics were back near normal from 15:04, and the checkout latency alert resolved at 15:07. The ticket records normal latency by 15:12 without intervention by the team. [provider-status:L8-L9] [checkout-metrics:L186-L194] [alerts-log:L10] [ticket:L19-L20]

## Best-supported cause

The best-supported explanation is **EU-1 authorization degradation, amplified by v2.14.0’s more patient payment retry profile**. The provider reported that some authorizations were not receiving a response during the incident window, and sampled slow traces directly show an 8-second payment timeout consuming nearly all of the checkout delay. [provider-status:L7-L9] [traces-2026-10-06:L335-L338]

Profile v18 raised the request timeout from 2,000 ms to 8,000 ms, increased the maximum attempts from two to four, and changed backoff from fixed to exponential. The traces show the 8-second timeout followed by a successful retry, consistent with those settings prolonging affected requests. Idempotency-key reuse remained enabled. [config-diff:L30-L47] [traces-2026-10-06:L336-L337]

Provider degradation was not unique to this release: on Oct 4, checkout p95 rose to about 4.2 seconds while v2.13.3/v17 was running, during a separately reported EU-1 provider incident. This supports the provider as an independent trigger; the evidence supports v18 as an amplifier, not the sole cause. [provider-status:L11-L14] [checkout-metrics:L32-L58]

## Competing explanation

**Orders-DB CPU/reindex is the main competing explanation, but the evidence does not support it as the primary cause of the multi-second checkout delays.** The reindex and high CPU overlapped the incident: CPU reached 80–92% during the reindex window, and the CPU alert fired at 14:15. [db-change-log:L7] [db-metrics:L132-L163] [alerts-log:L5]

However, during that window query p95 was 14–30 ms and pool-wait p95 was 1–3 ms; in the sampled slow trace, cart load and order persistence were only 24 ms and 30 ms, versus 8,562 ms in payment authorization. [db-metrics:L132-L163] [traces-2026-10-06:L332-L338] The Oct 4 provider-related latency spike also occurred with DB CPU at 26–38%, query p95 at 14–18 ms, and pool wait at 0–1 ms. [checkout-metrics:L32-L58] [db-metrics:L32-L58] The reindex could have contributed minor delay, but it does not explain the dominant wait shown in the traces.

## Recommended mitigation

**If the problem recurs and persists, recommend an incident-commander-approved rollback of only the payment-client runtime profile to v17**, rather than rolling back the full release. The runbook describes this as reversible and applicable within about 60 seconds. [runbook-payments:L10-L15] It would reduce the prolonged timeout/retry behavior while leaving code and the database migration untouched; weigh the faster failure behavior against the risk of more payment failures. [release-notes:L23-L24] [config-diff:L35-L44]

Keep fraud screening and idempotency protections unchanged. After any approved profile change, monitor checkout p95 and payment-client error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L19-L22] No production change was made during this read-only investigation. [ticket:L26-L29]

## Uncertainty

The provider reports rounded times, and the traces are samples rather than a complete accounting of all checkouts. [provider-status:L3] The evidence strongly localizes sampled slow requests to payment, but does not quantify the share of all incident requests attributable to provider degradation versus any smaller contribution from DB activity or other factors. The incident had resolved in the available evidence, so the profile rollback is a contingency recommendation, not an assertion that it should be applied now. [ticket:L19-L20]

Investigate why POST /checkout slowed after release v2.14.0; build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Evidence gathered
- Release v2.14.0 rollout began 2026-10-06 14:02:10; migration 0142 was applied at 14:02:55; all instances were healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04:00; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09:00. [release-notes:L11-L18]

[provider-status:L5-L9] Ticket says checkout latency was normal by 15:12 without intervention. [ticket:L17-L20]

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents

3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9|

11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |

## Timeline

- **14:02–14:09:** The v2.14.0 rollout began at 14:02:10, migration 0142 was applied at 14:02:55, and all instances were healthy with payment profile v18 loaded by 14:04. Post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L15-L18]
- **14:10 onward:** The scheduled orders-DB reindex ran until 14:41; its change record anticipated elevated CPU but no table locks and only a possible slight query-latency rise. [db-change-log:L7]
- **Approximately 14:18:** The payment provider’s reported EU-1 impact began. Checkout metrics were near normal at 14:18, then showed elevated latency from 14:19 onward; the checkout p95 alert fired at 14:22. [provider-status:L7-L9] [checkout-metrics:L140-L145] [alerts-log:L7]
- **14:22–14:24:** Sampled traces show the long part of slow checkouts was payment authorization: one took 8,562 ms, including an 8,005 ms timeout followed by a successful retry; another took 8,543 ms with the same timeout-then-success pattern. By comparison, cart load and order persistence took 16–24 ms, address validation 38–39 ms, and fraud screening 34–43 ms. A nearby checkout at 14:23 completed in 412 ms, including 288 ms for payment. [traces-2026-10-06:L331-L353]
- **14:51–15:09:** The provider identified a faulty acquirer connection pool at 14:51, drained affected nodes at 15:04, and reported the impact resolved at 15:09. Checkout metrics were back near normal from 15:04, and the checkout latency alert resolved at 15:07. The ticket records normal latency by 15:12 without intervention by the team. [provider-status:L8-L9] [checkout-metrics:L186-L194] [alerts-log:L10] [ticket:L19-L20]

## Best-supported cause

The best-supported explanation is **EU-1 authorization degradation, amplified by v2.14.0’s more patient payment retry profile**. The provider reported that some authorizations were not receiving a response during the incident window, and sampled slow traces directly show an 8-second payment timeout consuming nearly all of the checkout delay. [provider-status:L7-L9] [traces-2026-10-06:L335-L338]

Profile v18 raised the request timeout from 2,000 ms to 8,000 ms, increased the maximum attempts from two to four, and changed backoff from fixed to exponential. The traces show the 8-second timeout followed by a successful retry, consistent with those settings prolonging affected requests. Idempotency-key reuse remained enabled. [config-diff:L30-L47] [traces-2026-10-06:L336-L337]

Provider degradation was not unique to this release: on Oct 4, checkout p95 rose to about 4.2 seconds while v2.13.3/v17 was running, during a separately reported EU-1 provider incident. This supports the provider as an independent trigger; the evidence supports v18 as an amplifier, not the sole cause. [provider-status:L11-L14] [checkout-metrics:L32-L58]

## Competing explanation

**Orders-DB CPU/reindex is the main competing explanation, but the evidence does not support it as the primary cause of the multi-second checkout delays.** The reindex and high CPU overlapped the incident: CPU reached 80–92% during the reindex window, and the CPU alert fired at 14:15. [db-change-log:L7] [db-metrics:L132-L163] [alerts-log:L5]

However, during that window query p95 was 14–30 ms and pool-wait p95 was 1–3 ms; in the sampled slow trace, cart load and order persistence were only 24 ms and 30 ms, versus 8,562 ms in payment authorization. [db-metrics:L132-L163] [traces-2026-10-06:L332-L338] The Oct 4 provider-related latency spike also occurred with DB CPU at 26–38%, query p95 at 14–18 ms, and pool wait at 0–1 ms. [checkout-metrics:L32-L58] [db-metrics:L32-L58] The reindex could have contributed minor delay, but it does not explain the dominant wait shown in the traces.

## Recommended mitigation

**If the problem recurs and persists, recommend an incident-commander-approved rollback of only the payment-client runtime profile to v17**, rather than rolling back the full release. The runbook describes this as reversible and applicable within about 60 seconds. [runbook-payments:L10-L15] It would reduce the prolonged timeout/retry behavior while leaving code and the database migration untouched; weigh the faster failure behavior against the risk of more payment failures. [release-notes:L23-L24] [config-diff:L35-L44]

Keep fraud screening and idempotency protections unchanged. After any approved profile change, monitor checkout p95 and payment-client error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L19-L22] No production change was made during this read-only investigation. [ticket:L26-L29]

## Uncertainty

The provider reports rounded times, and the traces are samples rather than a complete accounting of all checkouts. [provider-status:L3] The evidence strongly localizes sampled slow requests to payment, but does not quantify the share of all incident requests attributable to provider degradation versus any smaller contribution from DB activity or other factors. The incident had resolved in the available evidence, so the profile rollback is a contingency recommendation, not an assertion that it should be applied now. [ticket:L19-L20]
